records.title: Have watchers track like computeds?
records.body:
It'd simplify watcher management a lot, and it'd make it work like a mirror image of `untrack`. It also would simplify implementations somewhat and mitigate some perf hazards around `Signal.subtle.{,un}watch`.

The idea is this:

- `watcher.track(body)`: Tracks any newly accessed signals in `body()`, and after `body()` returns/throws, removes any signals *not* accessed. Returns the result of `body()`'s evaluation. The idea is it mirrors `untrack(body)`.
- `watcher.reset()`: Equivalent to `watcher.track(() => {})`, useful for clearing all signals in the watcher.

To add to a watcher, simply `.get()` inside a `track`ed callback. And to remove, simply omit.

This would also remove the need for intermediate `Computed`s for such auto-tracking.

-----

This stands somewhat in opposition to some of what I've suggested in #178, in that the watcher *would* have to retain a list of signals it depends on. However, it'd simplify the internal execution model a bit:

- `Watcher`s track dependent `State`s.
- `Computed`s track dependent `Computed`s and `State`s.
- On all signals' `get`, add the signal to the current `Watcher` if not already present.
- On `Computed#get`, it recurses through its dependencies to wire everything up.
    - On `State` dependency, add the `State` to the current `Watcher` if not already present. If dirty, treat the parent `Computed` as dirty.
    - On `Computed` dependency, add the `Computed` to the current `Watcher` if not already present, and recurse into its children. If after that, the dependency `Computed` is treated as dirty already, treat the parent `Computed` as dirty.
    - If all of a parent `Computed`'s dependencies treat it as dirty, toss the children (removing descendant `State`s from the current `Watcher` and vice versa if necessary) and execute the `Computed`'s body. If the result is equal, treat the parent `Computed` as not dirty. Speculative descent can speed this up considerably, at cost to some memory churn (it may be worth putting this into the spec as well):
        1. Clone the current `Watcher`'s dependent `State` set and let this be the saved set.
        2. Descend into existing dependencies. If none of them treat this `Computed` to be dirty, return.
        3. Reference-swap the current `Watcher`'s dependent `State` set with the saved set. Now, the speculative set is the one saved and the old set is the one being added to.
        4. Execute this `Computed`'s body. Treat this `Computed`'s parent as dirty if and only if the result equals the previous result.
        5. For each `State` in the saved (speculative) set not in the (possibly updated) current `Watcher`'s dependent `State` set, remove the current `Watcher` from that `State`'s watcher set.
- Before executing the tracked call, save the watcher's `State` set and set it to an empty set.
- After executing the tracked call, diff the watcher's current signal set against the saved one, adding watchers to new signals' observing watcher sets and removing watchers from old signals' observing watcher sets.
    1. Push new ones to an intermediate list and remove retained ones from the saved set. This leaves the saved set with only old entries.
    2. Add the watcher to the new signals. It's okay to allow recursive `.track(...)` as the current set isn't accessed here.
    3. Remove the watcher from the old signals. It's okay to allow recursive `.track(...)` as the current set isn't accessed here.
    > Why wait? It avoids premature unwatch -> rewatch cycles when a signal is removed from one `Computed` but added to another in the same pass. Likewise, the add-before-remove order ensures external reference counters don't hit zero and result in recreation of anything.
- Persistent state needed:
    - A global "current watcher" field
    - A global "current computed" field
    - A per-watcher "watched states" set (iteration order observable)
    - A per-computed "watched signals" set (iteration order *not* observable)
    - A per-state "linked watchers" set (iteration order *not* observable)

records.title: Compiler: rejection codes for rules that are currently prose-only (or silent)
records.body:
## Problem

Several build-time rules are enforced only by documentation, or not at all. An agent that has not read
`docs/claude.txt` end to end will break them, and two of them fail **silently**.

## Proposed codes

| Suggested | Rule | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| `FLX-1002` | `@ExportService` interface methods must return `void` | doc-only today |
| `FLX-1008` | `auditLog` used on a node in a graph built without `addEventAudit(…)` | **silent**: builds fine, logs nothing |
| `FLX-1003` | handler/trigger missing `boolean` return | exists as `failBuildIfMissingBooleanReturn`; give it a code |
| `FLX-1004` | `@OnTrigger(dirty=false)` with no sibling on the same parent | usually a mistake — warning, not error |
| `FLX-1005` | duplicate node name, or one colliding with a generated identifier | |
| `FLX-1006` | `@Inject` service unresolved at build time | |
| `FLX-1007` | dependency cycle, printed as the path `a → b → c → a` | |

## `FLX-1008` is the one with a downstream consequence

A node that calls `auditLog` in a graph built without an audit level produces a log that is
**misleading**, not merely absent: the node is silent for a reason no reader can see, and no downstream
tool can distinguish it from a node that legitimately stayed quiet. The audit-log analyser has an entire
execution-classification model (`LOGGED` / `RAN_SILENTLY` / `MAY_HAVE_RUN` / …) built around not
over-claiming from silence; this case makes silence unattributable.

`FLX-1002` is second: it is currently learned only by reading `claude.txt`.

_Raised from `docs/proposals/upstream-asks.md` in the fluxtion audit-log analyser (UP-FLX-02)._

records.title: [PROCESS] Conduct M0 exit review
records.body:
## Goal

Make one bounded M0 exit decision from a frozen evidence baseline. This is a decision review, not a program to eliminate every known concern.

## Frozen baseline

Evaluate the accepted revival integration commit:

`3825e90801454ae3c35fcb4753a8262d7dfcabf8`

Evidence discovered after this baseline may clarify the decision, but does not automatically expand M0 scope or become an exit dependency.

## Finding classification

Every unresolved finding must be placed in exactly one bucket:

1. **Exit blocker** — blocks M0 only when evidence shows that it:
   - prevents a reproducible accepted-baseline build or required visible runtime exercise;
   - invalidates authoritative M0 audit evidence;
   - creates immediate security or monetary exposure in the required workflow; or
   - presents demonstrated data-loss/corruption risk in the required baseline exercise.
2. **Accepted risk** — real and documented, with an owner/follow-up issue and explicit operating boundary, but does not prevent M1.
3. **Backlog** — useful follow-up that does not affect the M0 exit decision.

New discoveries do **not** automatically become dependencies. They are classified once using the criteria above. Process improvements do not enter M0 unless they themselves meet the exit-blocker test.

## Bounded critical path

1. Complete clean-current visible runtime evidence in #5.
2. Reproduce or disprove the disappearing-road behavior in #8 on the frozen baseline.
3. Contain the immediate required-workflow installation exposure in #53.
4. Classify #54 and #55 as blockers only if evidence shows they prevent a trustworthy acceptance pass; otherwise record them as accepted risks or backlog.
5. Run the acceptance pass once and publish the decision. Do not open a new investigation cycle during closeout.

## Acceptance pass

After #53 makes the required commands safe to run:

- `npm run build-compat`
- `npm run test-compat`
- visible new city → planning project → road → implementation → clean save/shutdown → reload

Record failures and evidence once. A failed required step produces a named blocker or explicit NO-GO; it does not authorize unrelated archaeology.

## Decision output

Publish exactly one result:

- **GO** — no exit blocker remains.
- **CONDITIONAL GO** — no exit blocker remains; accepted risks have owners, boundaries, and follow-up issues. M1 may begin.
- **NO-GO** — one or more evidence-backed exit blockers remain, each with an exact unblock condition.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Frozen commit and authoritative evidence links are recorded
- [ ] Every unresolved finding is classified as Exit blocker, Accepted risk, or Backlog
- [ ] #5 visible runtime evidence is complete
- [ ] #8 is reproduced or disproved on the frozen baseline
- [ ] #53 immediate installation exposure has a safe operating boundary
- [ ] #54 and #55 receive evidence-backed blocker/non-blocker dispositions
- [ ] One bounded build/test/visible acceptance pass is recorded
- [ ] Known risks and follow-up owners are explicit
- [ ] GO, CONDITIONAL GO, or NO-GO is published for the product owner
- [ ] No newly discovered follow-up silently expands M0 scope

## Operating constraint

No additional process-framework work is required before this decision. The existing governance is sufficient to close M0.

records.title: [BUG][MTL] DSP firmware boot -110 on resume — only when HDMI is connected AND audio streams via the internal analog path during system suspend (regression)
records.body:
### Describe the bug
On a ThinkPad T14s Gen 5 (Meteor Lake, `sof-audio-pci-intel-mtl`, PCI `0000:00:1f.3`), the DSP fails to boot firmware with `-110` (ETIMEDOUT) **on resume from system suspend (S2idle)**, leaving audio permanently dead until a full reboot. Module reload, PCI remove/rescan, and driver unbind/rebind do **not** recover it — only a power-cycle does.

The trigger is very specific and **fully reproducible**: it requires an active playback stream on the **internal analog** path *while an HDMI/DP display is connected* at the moment of suspend.

### Reproduction — requires ALL THREE conditions simultaneously
1. An external display is **connected via HDMI/DP** (HDMI codec present in topology).
2. Audio is **actively streaming through the internal analog codec** (in my case a background `fluidsynth` keeps the analog PCM open continuously).
3. The system enters **suspend (S2idle)**.

→ On resume, the DSP wedges with `-110`.

### It is NOT reproducible if any one condition is removed (each verified):
| HDMI connected | Active stream path | Suspend | Result |
|---|---|---|---|
| Yes | Analog | Yes | **WEDGE (-110)** |
| **No** | Analog | Yes | OK |
| Yes | **HDMI** | Yes | OK |
| Yes | Analog | **No** | OK |

The monitor *model* is irrelevant — reproduced with two different external monitors in two locations. Only the *presence* of a connected HDMI sink matters. This points to a cross-codec suspend/resume ordering issue: resuming the active analog path fails only when an idle-but-present HDMI codec also exists in the topology.

### Regression
This worked correctly a few months ago — suspending with the same `fluidsynth` setup did not break audio. It has regressed since. (Happy to help bisect kernel / firmware versions to narrow the window.)

### dmesg on the failed resume / forced re-probe
```
sof-audio-pci-intel-mtl 0000:00:1f.3: Loaded firmware library: ADSPFW, version: 2.12.0.1
sof-audio-pci-intel-mtl 0000:00:1f.3: timeout waiting for purge IPC done
sof-audio-pci-intel-mtl 0000:00:1f.3: ------------[ DSP dump start ]------------
sof-audio-pci-intel-mtl 0000:00:1f.3: Boot iteration failed: 3/3
sof-audio-pci-intel-mtl 0000:00:1f.3: fw_state: SOF_FW_BOOT_IN_PROGRESS (3)
sof-audio-pci-intel-mtl 0000:00:1f.3: 0xd000001c: module: ROM_EXT, state: REMOVE_ACCESS_CONTROL, not running
sof-audio-pci-intel-mtl 0000:00:1f.3: error code: 0x2328 (unknown)
sof-audio-pci-intel-mtl 0000:00:1f.3: ------------[ DSP dump end ]------------
sof-audio-pci-intel-mtl 0000:00:1f.3: error: dsp init failed after 3 attempts with err: -110
sof-audio-pci-intel-mtl 0000:00:1f.3: Failed to start DSP
sof-audio-pci-intel-mtl 0000:00:1f.3: error: failed to boot DSP firmware -110
sof-audio-pci-intel-mtl 0000:00:1f.3: error: sof_probe_work failed err: -110
```
Note: the failure is at the **boot ROM** stage (`ROM_EXT / REMOVE_ACCESS_CONTROL`), before firmware runs — so no PCI/driver/PM-level recovery works; only a full power cycle resets the DSP.

### Environment
- **Hardware:** Lenovo ThinkPad T14s Gen 5 (21LS0041SG), BIOS `N46ET24W (1.14)`
- **SoC / audio:** Intel Meteor Lake, `sof-hda-dsp`, PCI `0000:00:1f.3`
- **Kernel:** `7.0.12+deb14.1-amd64` (Debian forky/sid)
- **SOF firmware:** `firmware-sof-signed 2025.01-1`; loaded ADSPFW `2.12.0.1`; `sof-mtl.ri`, IPC4
- **Topology:** `sof-ipc4-tplg/sof-hda-generic-2ch.tplg`
- **alsa-ucm-conf:** `1.2.16-1`
- **Userspace:** PipeWire + WirePlumber
- Suspend type: S2idle (modern standby)

### Possibly related
Same `-110`-on-suspend/resume IPC-timeout family: #1072, #2971, #4507, #4558 (different platforms/triggers, but similar resume failure signature).

### Additional context
I can reliably reproduce on demand and am happy to collect `sof-logger` traces, test patches, or bisect. Workarounds in the meantime: disconnect HDMI before suspend, or keep the system on AC (no auto-suspend).

records.title: [vm] JIT cross-function direct calls: CallDirect lowers to call_indirect on the callee NumericFn (spectral_norm 235x)
records.body:
The bytecode JIT bails an entire function back to the VM on any `Call` opcode — only `SelfCall` is lowered. `spectral_norm`'s `multiplyAv` calls `evalA` 20M times inside its inner loop, so none of the hot functions compile and the VM runs the benchmark at 10595ms vs node's 45ms (235x; machine-local measurement, darwin-arm64, node v24).

## Problem

The CFG JIT (`build_body_cfg`, `crates/tish_vm/src/jit.rs:657`) validates every opcode up front via `op_size` (`crates/tish_vm/src/jit.rs:629`), and `Call` is not in the table:

```rust
Some(match op {
    Nop | Pop | Dup | Return | LoopVarsEnd | EnterBlock | ExitBlock | GetIndex => 1,
    LoadLocal | StoreLocal | LoadConst | BinOp | UnaryOp | Jump | JumpIfFalse | JumpBack
    | LoopVarsBegin | SelfCall => 3,
    _ => return None,
})
```

`_ => return None` means a single cross-function call poisons the whole function; the only call shape that survives is `SelfCall` (arity-checked at `crates/tish_vm/src/jit.rs:685`). The doc comment at `crates/tish_vm/src/jit.rs:651` already *describes* direct-call lowering ("a `LoadVar name_idx` + `Call arity` where the callee has a `NumericFn` in `callees`"), but no such arm exists — it is aspirational and should be made true.

`tests/perf/spectral_norm.tish:11` is exactly this shape:

```text
for (let j = 0; j < n; j++) { sum = sum + evalA(i, j) * v[j] }
```

With n=1000, `multiplyAv` runs its inner kernel 20M times (and `multiplyAtv` another 20M), every `evalA` call going through the boxed interpreter call path.

The pieces needed already exist:

- Every `VmClosure` carries `jit_fn: Option<crate::jit::NumericFn>` (`crates/tish_vm/src/vm.rs:1026`), compiled eagerly at closure creation (`let jit_fn = crate::jit::try_compile_numeric(inner);`, `crates/tish_vm/src/vm.rs:1670`).
- That pointer is final: "The pointer is into a leaked, never-freed `JITModule`, so it is valid for the life of the process and safe to call from any thread" (`crates/tish_vm/src/jit.rs:36`).

## Proposed fix

Ride the `CallDirect(didx, argc)` opcode introduced by the call-path slimming work:

1. **Resolve at closure creation.** In the `Constant::Closure` arm (`crates/tish_vm/src/vm.rs:1661`), resolve each of the caller chunk's `CallDirect` entries to the callee's `VmClosure` and snapshot its `NumericFn` (if any) into a `direct_callees` table passed to `try_compile_numeric`.
2. **Lower in `build_body_cfg`.** Add `CallDirect` to `op_size`, and lower it to `call_indirect` on an `iconst`'d function pointer with an imported `argc x F64 -> F64` signature.
3. **Bail conservatively.** Callee not JIT'd, arity mismatch, `array_param_mask != 0`, or boolean result => whole-function bail to the VM. Correct, just slow.

```rust
// build_body_cfg — new arm alongside Opcode::SelfCall
Opcode::CallDirect => {
    let (didx, argc) = read_call_direct(code, ip)?;
    let nf = match direct_callees.get(didx) {
        Some(Some(nf)) if nf.arity() == argc && nf.array_param_mask() == 0
            && !nf.result_is_bool() => nf,
        _ => return None, // not JIT'd / arity / array params / bool → bail to VM
    };
    let sigref = f64_sig_for_arity(&mut bcx, argc);         // argc × F64 -> F64
    let ptr = bcx.ins().iconst(types::I64, nf.ptr() as i64); // FINAL: module never freed
    let args = pop_n(&mut stack, argc)?;
    let call = bcx.ins().call_indirect(sigref, ptr, &args);
    stack.push(bcx.inst_results(call)[0]);
}
```

Safety argument:

- `CallDirect` is only emitted where the compiler proves the callee binding is never reassigned program-wide (the call-path slimming contract), so the snapshotted pointer cannot go stale.
- Source order guarantees the callee's closure — and its `jit_fn` — exist before the caller's `LoadConst Closure` executes, so resolution at caller-creation time sees the final `NumericFn`.
- Mutual recursion: the later-defined callee does not exist when the earlier function is created => resolver miss => that caller bails to the VM. Correct, just slow; a second resolution pass is a possible follow-up if it ever matters.

## Expected impact

CallDirect lowering alone is not enough for spectral_norm: `multiplyAv` also reads `v[j]` and writes `av[i]`, so the caller loops only compile with array-JIT v2 (array writes in JIT'd loops). With both landed: spectral_norm ~10595ms -> **~60–120ms vs node 45** (machine-local). Honest range: cranelift will not auto-vectorize the inner kernel the way TurboFan does, so this is near-flip — the low end flips, the high end sits ~2.5x of node. Pure-numeric cross-function callers (no arrays) should see the full win from this issue alone.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Cross-backend parity suite green: tests/core, interp == vm == native == node.
- [ ] `tish run tests/perf/spectral_norm.tish` integer check identical to node's.
- [ ] Differential harness: vm (JIT on) == interp == node on direct-call fixtures covering mutual recursion, arity mismatch, runtime non-numeric args, boolean-result callees, and array-param callees — each must bail cleanly, never miscompile.
- [ ] Benchmark checksum-equality vs node: full gauntlet (`scripts/run_perf_gauntlet.sh`) unchanged, plus VM runs (`tish run`) of the affected benchmarks.
- [ ] No regression beyond run-to-run jitter on existing JIT wins (SelfCall recursion/fib, mandelbrot, fnv_hash).

## Effort / dependencies

**Effort: M–L.**

Depends on:

- [vm] call-path slimming (CallDirect) — introduces the opcode and the direct-call table this lowering consumes.
- [vm] array-JIT v2 — required for `multiplyAv`/`multiplyAtv` themselves to compile (array reads *and writes* in the caller loops); without it, CallDirect only helps pure-numeric callers.

Part of the Beat-Node performance roadmap (see tracking issue).

records.title: Investigate incremental AST scheduling for fixed-point type inference
records.body:
## Motivation

Type inference now runs to a fixed point, repeating inference passes until no persisted type facts change. Each round currently walks broad portions of the AST even when the previous round inferred only a small number of facts.

This is correct and keeps the implementation straightforward, but compilation performance may improve if subsequent rounds revisit only analysis regions that depend on newly inferred facts.

## Investigation

Explore an incremental/worklist-based inference strategy that:

- records which bindings, fields, callable parameters, callable returns, and object shapes changed in a round
- tracks the AST regions or inference nodes that depend on those facts
- schedules only affected scopes, call sites, expressions, or object-shape analyses for the next round
- avoids rebuilding parent/scope maps and repeatedly walking unrelated subtrees
- preserves deterministic convergence and repeated-state detection
- retains conservative JavaScript semantics, including hoisting, TDZ, definite initialization, conflicting call sites, and dynamic fallback

## Possible approaches

- Build a dependency graph between inferred facts and inference consumers.
- Use a worklist keyed by scope, callable, binding, or analysis kind.
- Cache stable AST parent/scope maps across rounds.
- Record invalidation edges while analyzing expressions and call sites.
- Begin with coarse scope-level invalidation, then measure whether finer-grained expression-level scheduling is worthwhile.

## Measurement

Compare the current full-round fixed-point implementation with candidate incremental approaches using:

- compiler phase timing and allocation measurements
- inference-heavy integration fixtures such as PrimeJavaScript and Dromaeo scenarios
- synthetic long dependency chains that require many convergence rounds
- unchanged generated IL and execution results

## Acceptance criteria

- Demonstrate a meaningful reduction in inference compilation time or allocation on hosted, repeatable benchmarks.
- Preserve all existing type-inference, generator, execution, and test262 behavior.
- Keep the implementation understandable and maintainable; do not trade correctness for marginal compilation gains.

## Priority

Low. The current fixed-point implementation is correct; this issue is a performance investigation and should be driven by measurements.

records.title: SDLC_ISSUE_NUMBER goes stale within a long-lived dev session, silently pointing downstream stages at the wrong issue
records.body:
<!-- draft-owner: pid=66869 ts=1786998543 -->
> **Context for a reader new to this repo.** This system runs an SDLC pipeline as a sequence of skills (`/do-plan`, `/do-build`, `/do-pr-review`, `/do-merge`, ...). Those skills run inside a long-lived **AgentSession** — a Redis-backed record of one conversational agent process. The session's environment is assembled in [`agent/sdk_client.py`](../blob/main/agent/sdk_client.py) by `_extract_sdlc_env_vars`, which derives a set of `SDLC_*` env vars from fields on the session record. One of those, `SDLC_ISSUE_NUMBER`, is supposed to tell a downstream stage which GitHub issue the current work belongs to.
>
> A **PM-driven dev session** is a single AgentSession that a PM (project manager) session routes many different tasks to over hours or days. It is not one-issue-scoped.

## Problem

`SDLC_ISSUE_NUMBER` is derived once, from a single session-level field, and then goes stale. Every downstream stage that trusts it un-guarded reads the wrong issue.

### Mechanism

`agent/sdk_client.py::_extract_sdlc_env_vars` (around lines 490-498):

```python
# Issue URL -> SDLC_ISSUE_NUMBER and SDLC_TRACKING_ISSUE
issue_url = getattr(session, "issue_url", None)
if isinstance(issue_url, str) and issue_url:
    issue_match = _ISSUE_NUMBER_RE.search(issue_url)
    if issue_match:
        issue_num = issue_match.group(1)
        env["SDLC_ISSUE_NUMBER"] = issue_num
        env["SDLC_TRACKING_ISSUE"] = issue_num
```

That is a one-shot read of one `AgentSession` field. But a PM-driven dev session serves **many** issues over its lifetime. `session.issue_url` holds whatever it was when the session record was last written — in practice the **first** issue the session ever touched — and it is never re-derived per routed task.

### Current behavior (directly observed, 2026-08-18)

`SDLC_ISSUE_NUMBER` read `2734` on three consecutive runs, including runs routed for issue #2741 and issue #2636. Verified in-session: the env var held `2734` while the routed work was PR #2833 / issue #2636. Issue #2734 is an unrelated open issue about reflections registry integrity.

### Blast radius

The guarded path is safe. [`.claude/skills-global/do-pr-review/sub-skills/checkout.md`](../blob/main/.claude/skills-global/do-pr-review/sub-skills/checkout.md) (lines ~27-49) correctly treats the env var as **LAST RESORT**, behind PR-body `Closes #N` / `tracking:` extraction, per #1731 — and `tests/unit/test_sdlc_fork_issue_number.py` enforces that ordering.

Two consumers are **un-guarded**:

| Site | Use | Consequence when stale |
|------|-----|------------------------|
| `.claude/skills-global/do-pr-review/sub-skills/code-review.md:47-49` | `gh issue view $SDLC_ISSUE_NUMBER` | The reviewer reads the **wrong issue's acceptance criteria** and judges the PR against them |
| `.claude/skills-global/do-pr-review/sub-skills/post-review.md:221` | `git commit -m "docs(#${SDLC_ISSUE_NUMBER}): sync plan checkboxes with review verdict"` | Plan-checkbox sync commit is attributed to the wrong issue |

Worse: any stage that runs **before a PR exists** has no PR body to fall back on, so it has no correction available at all. The `checkout.md` mitigation only exists because a PR body happens to be present at review time.

### Failure mode

Silent cross-issue state corruption. A verdict, a plan-checkbox sync, or a stage marker gets recorded against issue #2734 while the actual work is issue #2636. Nothing errors, nothing warns; the wrong lane's substrate is mutated and the right lane's is left un-updated. Detection is by coincidence.

## Desired outcome

No stage can ever read an issue number that does not correspond to the task it was routed. Either the value is correct for the current task, or it is absent and the stage fails loudly.

## Definitions

| Term | Meaning |
|------|---------|
| **AgentSession** | Redis-backed record of one long-lived agent process; carries `issue_url`, `plan_url`, `slug`, etc. See [`docs/features/eng-session-architecture.md`](../blob/main/docs/features/eng-session-architecture.md) |
| **Routed task** | One unit of work a PM session hands to a dev session; many routed tasks share one AgentSession |
| **Ambient env var** | A value injected into the subprocess environment rather than passed explicitly as an argument — implicit, unversioned, and invisible at the call site |
| **Lane** | One issue's end-to-end pipeline run (task list + branch + worktree + plan doc). See [`docs/features/sdlc-lane-identity.md`](../blob/main/docs/features/sdlc-lane-identity.md) |

## Solution sketch (open questions, not a chosen approach)

Two directions, and the plan should decide between them rather than assume:

1. **Re-derive per routed task.** Make the issue number a property of the task being dispatched, not of the session record — recompute it at each stage dispatch. Keeps the env var but makes it truthful. Open question: what is the authoritative per-task source, and does every dispatch path have it?

2. **Delete the ambient export entirely.** Stop exporting `SDLC_ISSUE_NUMBER` / `SDLC_TRACKING_ISSUE` from `_extract_sdlc_env_vars` and make every consumer resolve the issue number explicitly (skill args, PR body, or an explicit lookup that fails loudly on ambiguity). This is the direction #1731 already set for `/do-sdlc`: `tests/unit/test_sdlc_fork_issue_number.py:375-394` asserts do-sdlc must **NOT** export it — the env var in `sdk_client.py` is the surviving remnant of the same anti-pattern one layer down.

Direction 2 appears more consistent with the existing precedent, but the plan must enumerate every consumer of `SDLC_ISSUE_NUMBER` and `SDLC_TRACKING_ISSUE` (skills, hooks, tools, tests) before committing, and decide what an unresolvable issue number should do at each site.

Open questions for `/do-plan`:
- Which pre-PR stages currently depend on the ambient value with no fallback?
- Is `SDLC_TRACKING_ISSUE` (same one-shot derivation) consumed anywhere, and does it have the same staleness exposu

records.title: Scan blob references from every stored ecosystem
records.body:
## Problem

Blob reclamation and backup both treat the registered `BlobReferenceDriver`s as the complete inventory of live
digests. [`referenced_blob_digests_with_drivers`](https://github.com/tox-dev/peryx/blob/main/crates/peryx/src/app/purge.rs#L75-L81)
folds [`blob_reference_drivers()`](https://github.com/tox-dev/peryx/blob/main/crates/peryx-driver/src/driver_set.rs#L81-L83)
into one set and returns it. That driver set is a projection of the configuration file:
[`activate_plugins`](https://github.com/tox-dev/peryx/blob/main/crates/peryx/src/server.rs#L106-L113) activates the
ecosystems named by `config.indexes`, and the cache CLI hands exactly that set to the purge
([`cache_with_plugins`](https://github.com/tox-dev/peryx/blob/main/crates/peryx/src/app/cache.rs#L28-L44)).

The metadata store is not a projection of the configuration. Every configured index gets a persisted repository record
carrying its ecosystem ([`reconcile_configured_repositories`](https://github.com/tox-dev/peryx/blob/main/crates/peryx/src/config/repository_migration.rs#L30-L41)),
and [`reconcile_repositories`](https://github.com/tox-dev/peryx/blob/main/crates/peryx-storage/src/meta/repository.rs#L388-L398)
retains the records of routes the configuration no longer names. Each ecosystem's own scan walks the whole store rather
than a route list, so an unregistered ecosystem does not fail the scan - it contributes nothing.

The short set reaches three destructive surfaces.
[`purge_orphaned_blobs`](https://github.com/tox-dev/peryx/blob/main/crates/peryx-ha-distributed/src/reclaim_guard.rs#L71-L84)
deletes every blob outside it while the metadata rows that referenced them survive;
[`copy_referenced_blobs`](https://github.com/tox-dev/peryx/blob/main/crates/peryx/src/operator/backup.rs#L141-L152)
writes a backup whose `metadata/peryx.redb` holds records the backup's `blobs.tsv` and `blobs/` have no bytes for; and
[`check_metadata_references`](https://github.com/tox-dev/peryx/blob/main/crates/peryx/src/operator/verify.rs#L297-L313)
re-derives the expected digests through the same restricted driver set, so `peryx backup verify` prints `ok`. The loss
surfaces at restore.

Nothing downstream can catch it. [`orphan_candidates`](https://github.com/tox-dev/peryx/blob/main/crates/peryx-ha-distributed/src/reclaim_guard.rs#L112-L133)
applies no age, ownership, or ecosystem filter, and the re-scan before the guard arms calls the same truncated closure,
so the recheck reproduces the same short set. The running server builds its distributed inventory the same way:
[`prepare_distributed_availability`](https://github.com/tox-dev/peryx/blob/main/crates/peryx/src/process.rs#L107-L123)
hands `plugins.drivers()` to `reference_inventory`, so distributed reclamation inherits the projection. Re-adding the
index later restores the routes, not the bytes.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    A[Config names PyPI only] --> B[Activate PyPI driver]
    B --> C[Live digest set covers PyPI]
    D[Store holds OCI manifests and blobs] --> E[No OCI driver to scan]
    C --> F[OCI blobs armed as orphans]
    E --> F
    F --> G[Blobs deleted, OCI metadata retained]
    class A,B,C,D,F accent
    class E,G warn
    classDef accent fill:#dbe6f5,stroke:#4a6f9f,color:#16304d
    classDef warn fill:#f6e2d0,stroke:#b06f36,color:#5a3212
```

## Example

A server runs one PyPI index and one OCI index. An operator decommissions the OCI route by removing it from
`peryx.toml` - or runs maintenance from a trimmed config - and runs `peryx cache purge orphaned-blobs --yes`. Only the
PyPI driver is registered, so every layer and manifest blob reachable solely through OCI metadata falls outside
`live_digests` and is deleted, while its OCI repository, manifest, and descriptor rows stay in the store. The same
config makes `peryx backup create` write a backup missing those bytes and `peryx backup verify` print `ok` over it.

## Required change

- Derive the ecosystems a reference scan must cover from the metadata store, not from the activated plugin set; the
  `ecosystem` field on stored repository records is the durable evidence.
- Make the reference scan fail, naming every ecosystem present in the store with no registered `BlobReferenceDriver`, so
  `cache purge orphaned-blobs`, `backup create`, and `backup verify` refuse rather than proceed on a short inventory.
- Expose the presence check as a narrow capability on the plugin contract, so the registry can ask whether the store
  holds records of an ecosystem it did not activate without the binary branching per ecosystem.
- Apply the same refusal to the reference inventory handed to distributed reclamation, not only to the CLI collector.
- Keep the dry-run path usable: it reports the refusal instead of listing another ecosystem's blobs as reclaimable.
- Report the covered ecosystems in the purge and backup output so a completed scan names its own scope.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] With repositories from two ecosystems in the store and a config naming one, `peryx cache purge orphaned-blobs
      --yes` exits non-zero, deletes no blob, and names the uncovered ecosystem.
- [ ] The same config makes `peryx backup create` fail instead of writing a backup whose metadata references digests
      absent from `blobs.tsv`.
- [ ] `peryx backup verify` reports a problem for a backup whose `blobs.tsv` omits a digest referenced by an ecosystem
      it cannot scan.
- [ ] The dry-run reports the refusal and names the uncovered ecosystem instead of listing its blobs as reclaimable.
- [ ] Distributed reclamation refuses the same configuration rather than reclaiming against a partial inventory.
- [ ] A config covering every ecosystem present in the store leaves all three commands succeeding as today.

## Architecture and test boundary

Keep shared code ecosystem-neutral. Shared crates must not depend on concrete `peryx-ecosystem-*` crates or add
PyPI/OCI branches. When a shared workflow needs ecosystem behavior, expose a narrow capability trait fr

records.title: Recursive-CTE work queue is a comparison-keyed ephemeral B-tree index; SQLite uses an integer-keyed table
records.body:
```sql
WITH RECURSIVE s(i) AS (SELECT 1 UNION ALL SELECT i+1 FROM s WHERE i<100000) SELECT count(*) FROM s;
```

```
turso                                          sqlite
3|OpenEphemeral|1|0|0| cursor=1 is_table=false 3|OpenEphemeral|2|1|0| nColumn=1; Queue table
7|MakeRecord|4|2|6| … for recursive-queue-s    6|NewRowid|2|5|0
8|IdxInsert|1|6|0||8    <- record-comparison   7|Insert|2|4|5      <- append, no comparison
                           seek per push
9|Rewind|1|24
11|IdxDelete|1|7|2      <- index delete per pop 11|Delete|2|0|0
```

Every push pays a record encode plus a comparison descent; every pop pays a full index delete. SQLite appends to a rowid table.

| N | turso | sqlite |
|---|---|---|
| 25k | 902 ms | 8 ms |
| 50k | 1702 ms | 13 ms |
| 100k | 3439 ms | 22 ms |
| 200k | 7099 ms | 40 ms |

Linear in both engines. Turso-vs-turso: 100k queue iterations = 3439 ms against a plain 100k-row B-tree table scan at **32 ms** — ~107× per row inside the same build. `gdb` sampling of this case (the queue holds one row, so the debug-only cell validator is nearly free here) lands on real work: `op_idx_insert → seek_internal → indexbtree_seek_inner → compare_with_current_record → compare_records_int`, and `op_idx_delete → btree delete → restore_context / add_dirty → subjournal_page_if_required`. None of those are `cfg(debug_assertions)`.

Root cause: `core/translate/recursive_cte.rs:79-103`. `queue_index_columns` gets priority columns only when `recursive_cte.queue_order` is `Some`; in the common case the key is just `sequence` + result columns. But the queue is **always** built as `Index { unique: true, has_rowid: false, … }` with `CursorType::BTreeIndex` and `OpenEphemeral { is_table: false }`. A monotonically increasing `sequence` prefix makes this a FIFO that pays comparison-based insertion for no benefit.

Fix: when `recursive_cte.queue_order.is_none()`, emit `QueryDestination::EphemeralTable` with `NewRowid`/`Insert`/`Delete`, matching SQLite's Queue table. Keep the index form only for genuine priority queues.

Caveat on magnitude: this was measured on a debug build, where `debug_validate_cells_core` (`core/storage/btree.rs:9415`, `cfg(debug_assertions)`) re-walks every cell on a page on each insert and balance step. For *deep, wide* traversals where the queue grows to thousands of rows, profiling shows most of the time back inside that validator, so those larger ratios are mostly the build. The structural difference (index vs table) and the 107× against a same-build scan control are not.

records.title: Epic: Conditional components and transactional dependency graph reconfiguration
records.body:
## Goal

Create a first-class conditional component system that can select, enable, disable, replace, and reconstruct components and trait providers when runtime facts change, especially configuration values and dependency/provider availability.

The system must build on Upwell's existing component descriptors, factory metadata, dependency graph, `Live` / `Dep<T>` slots, transactional config reload, and generic hook infrastructure. It must not introduce a parallel container or a second reload pipeline.

## Motivation

Applications often ship a safe default implementation while allowing an application-specific implementation only under particular conditions.

For example, an injectable `Authenticator` trait may have:

- a framework default provider that is always eligible as a fallback;
- an application provider that is eligible only while `auth.custom.enabled = true`;
- consumers that either inject `Dep<dyn Authenticator>` and can follow a live provider slot, or hold fixed dependencies and must be reconstructed when the selected provider changes.

If the application starts with the flag enabled and a config reload changes it to `false`, Upwell should derive the next effective graph, determine the affected reverse-dependency closure, let each affected component declare whether it can absorb the change or requires replacement, prepare any replacements, run hooks, and atomically publish the new configuration and component graph. A failed transition must leave the previous configuration and graph active.

## Current baseline

- `ComponentDescriptor` exposes static factory, dependency, condition, and source metadata.
- Multiple factories already support an explicit factory with a default fallback, but selection is currently static.
- `ProviderDescriptor` represents trait-provider selection and has a stable structural mapping identity.
- `DependencyDescriptor` distinguishes `Snapshot` and `Live` observation.
- `Live<T>` / `Dep<T>` provides a shared runtime-swappable slot; existing tests prove multiple consumers observe replacement while old snapshots remain valid.
- `Cfg<T>` uses the same live-slot model for committed config values.
- `ConditionCatalog` validates and evaluates supplied typed fact snapshots without constructing components.
- DI condition, selection, construction-edge, build-order, and cycle decisions emit structured redacted tracing.
- `ConfigReloader` stages changed bindings and commits only after preparation and hooks succeed, but does not yet coordinate a whole runtime generation.
- `AppRuntime` retains resolved component and scope plans, but does not yet own a graph-transition coordinator.

## Required model

### Conditions

Conditions are declarative and inspectable. The v1 contract supports typed config boolean/equality facts, component and exact provider-mapping eligibility, logical composition, and metadata-declared trusted config/availability callbacks whose framework inputs remain statically declared. Availability cycles are rejected deterministically with stable paths.

### Effective graph transitions

A change must produce explicit before/after effective graphs and a deterministic transition plan. The planner distinguishes retain, live rebind, replace, add, and remove. Fixed `Arc<T>` or by-value consumers must not silently retain stale dependencies.

### Component-controlled replacement

Each affected component declares its transition policy. Reconstruction may use the ordinary factory, a static state-aware factory, or a transition-local one-shot factory while resolving only against proposed state.

### Transactionality

Config, component/provider bindings, effective graph metadata, and future scope plans publish as one runtime generation after all validation, hooks, and construction succeed. Any failure preserves the complete previous generation.

### Hooks and observability

Users need deterministic redacted proposal, decision, commit, abort, and displacement reports through the generic hooks system. Current DI graph-decision tracing provides low-level condition, selection, build-edge, cycle, and build-order diagnostics; transition-level reports remain #211.

## Scope and lifecycle constraints

- Runtime activation and replacement remain singleton-focused in v1.
- Existing open scopes pin their generation; future root-based openings use current state.
- Provider changes preserve the authoritative qualifier, primary, ordering, cardinality, and scope model.
- Tooling mode may project static metadata but must not construct components or execute trusted callbacks.
- Runtime transition serialization prevents stale-generation commits.

## Sub-issues

- [x] #204 Conditional components: semantics and deterministic evaluation
- [x] #210 Conditional components: descriptor and registry metadata
- [x] #207 Conditional components: graph diff and impact planning
- [ ] #209 Conditional components: component-owned transition strategies
- [ ] #206 Conditional components: transactional config and graph commit
- [ ] #211 Conditional components: hooks, reports, and observability
- [ ] #208 Conditional components: macro and builder ergonomics
- [ ] #205 Conditional components: tooling, lifecycle hardening, and performance

## Acceptance criteria

- A default `Authenticator` provider and a config-gated custom provider can switch in both directions at runtime.
- The candidate graph and affected reverse-dependency closure are deterministic and inspectable before commit.
- `Dep<dyn Authenticator>` consumers observe a compatible provider replacement without mandatory reconstruction.
- Fixed consumers are reconstructed or the transition is rejected; stale fixed dependencies are never silently retained.
- A component can choose hot update, ordinary reconstruction, static state-aware reconstruction, or a transition-local factory under a documented contract.
- Config, provider selection, component slots, graph metadata, and future scope plans publish as one generation.
- Any failure preserves
